practice.e: The spelling practice is attested once in Middle English for both the noun and the verb. The noun began to be assimilated in spelling to nouns in -ice; practise (noun) is now obsolete.
practice.g: Repetition of an activity to improve a skill.

practise.e: From Middle English practizen, a variant of practisen, from Middle French pratiser, practiser, from Medieval Latin practizo, from Late Latin practico (“to do, perform, execute, propose, practise, exercise, be conversant with, contrive, conspire, etc.”), from prāctica (“practical affairs", "business”), from Ancient Greek πρᾱκτική (prāktikḗ).
practise.g: To repeat (an activity) as a way of improving one's skill in that activity.

practitioner.e: Formerly practicioner for *practicianer, from practician + -er (the suffix unnecessarily added, as in musicianer).
practitioner.g: A person who practices a profession or art, especially law or medicine.

praise.e: From Middle English praise, preyse, from the verb (see below).
From Middle English praisen, preisen, from Old French proisier, preisier (“to value, prize”), from Late Latin pretiō (“to value, prize”) from pretium (“price, worth, reward”).
praise.g: To give praise to; to commend, glorify, or worship.

praiseworthy.g: Meriting praise; worthy of high praise

prance.e: From Middle English prancen, prauncen (“to prance”, literally “to show off”), variant of Middle English pranken (“to prank”), thus probably from the same ultimate root as prank.
prance.g: To spring forward on the hind legs.

prate.e: From Middle English praten; either inherited from Old English prætt or borrowed via Middle Dutch or Middle Low German praten (from Old Saxon *pratt), all from Proto-West Germanic *prattu, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *prattuz (“idle or boastful talk, deceit”), from Proto-Indo-European *bred- (“to wander, rove”).
prate.g: Talk to little purpose; trifling talk; unmeaningful loquacity.

pray.e: From Middle English preien, borrowed from Anglo-Norman preier, from Old French proiier, from Late Latin precāre, from Latin precārī, from prex (“request, petition, prayer”), from Proto-Italic *preks, from Proto-Indo-European *preḱ- (“to request, ask”).
pray.g: To direct words, thoughts, or one's attention to a deity or any higher being, for the sake of adoration, thanks, petition for help, etc.

pray.e: Ellipsis of I pray you, I pray thee, whence also prithee.
pray.g: Please; used to make a polite request

prayer.e: From Middle English preiere, from Old French preiere, from Early Medieval Latin precāria, derived from Latin precem.
prayer.g: A practice of communicating with one's God, or with some spiritual entity.

preach.e: From Middle English prechen, from Old French prëechier, precchier (Modern French prêcher), from Latin praedicō (“to proclaim, announce”, literally “to fore-assign, pre-dedicate”).

preacher.e: From Middle English precher, prechere; partly equivalent to preach + -er, and partly continuing Middle English prechour, prechiour, from Old French preecheor (French prêcheur), from Latin praedicator (“public praiser, proclaimer”).
preacher.g: Someone who preaches a worldview, philosophy, or religion, especially someone who preaches the gospel and especially a clergyman or clergywo

preaching.g: The act of delivering a sermon or similar moral instruction.

precede.e: From Middle French précéder, from Latin praecēdō, from prae- + cēdō.
precede.g: To go before, go in front of.

preceding.e: From Middle English precedyng, precedenge, present participle of Middle English preceden (“to precede”), equivalent to precede + -ing.
preceding.g: Occurring before or in front of something else, in time, place, rank or sequence.

precept.e: Borrowed from Late Latin praeceptum, form of praecipiō (“to teach”), from Latin prae (“pre-”) + capiō (“take”).
precept.g: A rule or principle, especially one governing personal conduct.

precious.e: From Middle English precious, borrowed from Old French precios (“valuable, costly, precious, beloved, also affected, finical”), from Latin pretiōsus (“of great value, costly, dear, precious”), from pretium (“value, price”); see price.

predecessor.e: From Middle English predecessour, from Old French predecesseor (“forebear”), from Late Latin praedēcessor, from Latin prae- (“pre-”) + Latin dēcessor (“retiring officer”), from Latin dēcēdō (“to retire, to die”) (English decease).
predecessor.g: One who precedes; one who has preceded another in any state, position, office, etc.; one whom another follows or comes after, in any office

predestinate.e: From Middle English predestinate, from Latin praedestinātus, past participle of praedestināre. By surface analysis, pre- + destinate.

predestine.e: From Old French prédestiner, from Medieval Latin praedestinare. By surface analysis, pre- + destine.
predestine.g: To determine the future or the fate of something in advance; to preordain.

predict.e: Early 17th century, from Latin praedicō (“to mention beforehand”) (perfect passive participle praedictus), from prae- (“before”) + dīcō (“to say”). Equivalent to Germanic forespeak, foretell, and foresay.
predict.g: To make a prediction: to forecast, foretell, or estimate a future event on the basis of knowledge and reasoning; to prophesy a future event

prediction.e: Borrowed from Latin praedictiō, praedictiōnis; equivalent to predict + -ion.
prediction.g: A statement of what will happen in the future.

preeminence.g: The status of being preeminent, dominant or ascendant.

preeminent.e: Borrowed from Middle French preeminent and its source, Latin praeēminēns, present participle of praeēmineō (“to stand out, excel”), from prae- (“pre-”) + ēmineō.
preeminent.g: Exceeding others in quality or rank; of outstanding excellence, extremely notable or important.

prefect.e: From Middle English prefect and prefecte, from Old French prefect (Mod. French préfet), from Latin praefectus (“one placed in charge, overseer, director, prefect”), from praeficere (“to place in charge”).
prefect.g: An official of Ancient Rome who controlled or superintended a particular command, charge, department, etc.

prefer.e: From Middle English preferren, from Anglo-Norman preferer, from Latin praeferō.
prefer.g: To be in the habit of choosing something rather than something else; to favor; to like better.

pregnancy.g: The condition of being pregnant; an instance of this.

pregnant.e: From Middle English preignant, from Old French preignant, pregnant, also prenant (compare archaic Modern French prégnant), and their source, Latin praegnāns (“pregnant”), probably from prae- (“pre-”) + *gnāscī, an archaic form of nāscī (“to be born”).
pregnant.g: Carrying developing offspring within the body.

pregnant.e: Apparently from Middle French pregnant, preignant (“pressing, compelling”), present participle of prembre (“to press”), from Latin premere (“to press”).

premeditate.e: Borrowed from Latin praemeditātus, past participle of praemeditor (“to premeditate”). By surface analysis, pre- + meditate.
premeditate.g: To meditate, consider, or plan beforehand; to think about and revolve in the mind beforehand.

preparation.e: From Middle English preparacion, from Middle French preparacion, from Latin praeparatio, praeparationem. Morphologically prepare + -ation.
preparation.g: The act of preparing or getting ready.

prepare.e: Partially a back-formation from preparation; and partially borrowed from Middle French preparer, from Classical Latin praeparāre (“make ready in advance”), from prae- (“pre-”) + parāre (“make ready”).
prepare.g: To make ready for a specific future purpose; to set up; to assemble or equip; to forearm.

presbytery.e: From Middle English presbetory, presbytory (“part of church reserved for clergy”), from Late Latin presbyterium (“group of presbyters, part of church reserved for clergy”), from Ancient Greek πρεσβῠτέρῐον (presbŭtérĭon, “group of presbyters”), from πρεσβῠ́τερος (presbŭ́teros, “elder, priest”) + -ῐον (-ĭon). By surface analysis, presbyter + -y.
presbytery.g: The home of a Roman Catholic parish priest.

prescribe.e: Borrowed from Latin praescrībere, from prae- (“before, in front”) and scrībere (“to write”).
prescribe.g: To order (a drug or medical device) for use by a particular patient (under licensed authority).

presence.e: Through Old French presence, from Latin praesentia (“a being present”), from praesentem.
presence.g: The fact or condition of being present, or of being within sight or call, or at hand.

present.e: From Middle English present, from Old French present, from Latin praesent-, praesens, present participle of praeesse (“to be present”), from Latin prae- (“pre-”) + esse (“to be”).
present.g: Relating to now, for the time being; current.

present.e: From Middle English presenten, from Old French presenter, from Latin praesentāre (“to show”), from praesent-, praesens, present participle of praeesse (“be in front of”).
present.g: A gift, especially one given for birthdays, Christmas, anniversaries, graduations, weddings, or any other special occasions.

presentable.e: From Middle French presentable, from Old French, as if present + -able.
presentable.g: In good enough shape to be shown or offered to other people; tidy; attractive.

presently.e: From Middle English presently; equivalent to present + -ly.

preservation.e: From Old French preservacion, from Medieval Latin preservatio. Morphologically preserve + -ation.
preservation.g: The act of preserving; care to preserve; act of keeping from destruction, decay or any ill.

preserve.e: From Middle English preserven, from Old French preserver, from Medieval Latin prēservāre (“keep, preserve”), from Late Latin praeservāre (“guard beforehand”), from prae (“before”, adverb) + servāre (“maintain, keep”).
preserve.g: A sweetened spreadable jam or jelly made of any of a variety of fruits, such as strawberry, peach, or apple.

preside.e: From Old French presider, from Latin praesidēre (“preside”), from pre- (“before”) + sedere (“to sit”).
preside.g: To act as president or chairperson.

president.e: From Old French president, from Latin praesidēns (“presiding over; president, leader”) (accusative: praesidentem). The Latin word is the substantivized present active participle of the verb praesideō (“preside over”). The original meaning of the verb is 'to sit before' in the sense of presiding at a meeting.
president.g: The head of state of a republic, sometimes also the head of government as well, particularly (US politics) the head of the executive branch

press.e: From Middle English presse (“throng, crowd, clothespress”), partially from Old English press (“clothespress”) (from Medieval Latin pressa) and from Old French presse (Modern French presse) from Old French presser (“to press”), from Latin pressāre, from pressus, past participle of premere (“to press”).
press.g: An instance of applying pressure; an instance of pressing.

press.e: From Middle English pressen (“to crowd, thring, press”), from Old French presser (“to press”) (Modern French presser) from Latin pressāre, from pressus, past participle of premere "to press".
press.g: To exert weight or force against, to act upon with force or weight; to exert pressure upon.

presume.e: From Middle English presumen, from Anglo-Norman presumer and its source, Latin praesūmere (“to take beforehand, anticipate”), from prae- + sūmere (“to take”).
presume.g: To be so presumptuous as (to do something) without proper authority or permission [with to (+ infinitive)].

presumption.e: From pre- + Latin sūmptus + -ion, from Middle English presumpcioun, presumption, from Old French presumption and its etymon Latin praesūmptiō.
presumption.g: The act of presuming, or something presumed.

presumptuous.e: From Middle English presumptuous, borrowed from Old French presumpcieus, presumptieus, presumptuos and its etymon Medieval Latin praesūmptuōsus.
presumptuous.g: Making unwarranted presumptions or assumptions, often out of arrogance or excessive self-confidence, and thus exceeding appropriate or right

pretend.e: From Anglo-Norman pretendre, Middle French pretendre (French prétendre (“to claim, demand”)), from Latin praetendere (“to put forward, hold out, pretend”), from prae- (“pre-”) + tendō (“stretch”); see tend.
pretend.g: To speak or behave so as to give a false or simulated appearance.

pretense.e: Borrowed from Middle French pretensse, from Late Latin praetēnsus, past participle of Latin praetendō (“to pretend”), from prae- (“before”) + tendō (“to stretch”); see pretend.
pretense.g: The action of pretending; false or simulated show or appearance; false or hypocritical assertion or representation.

pretentious.e: From French prétentieux, from prétention, from Latin praetēnsus (“false or hypocritical profession”), past participle of praetendō. Note that pretentious is spelled with a ‘t’, unlike related pretense, pretension. This is due to the French spelling: *-sious does not occur as an English suffix, though -sion and -tion both do.
pretentious.g: Motivated by an inappropriate, excessive, or unjustified desire to impress others.

pretext.e: From Latin praetextum (“an ornament, etc., wrought in front, a pretense”), neuter of praetextus, past participle of praetexere (“to weave before, fringe or border, allege”).
pretext.g: A false, contrived, or assumed purpose or reason; a pretense.

prevail.e: From Middle English prevailen, from Old French prevaler, from Latin praevaleō (“be very able or more able, be superior, prevail”), from prae (“before”) + valeō (“be able or powerful”).
prevail.g: To be superior in strength, dominance, influence, or frequency; to have or gain the advantage over others; to have the upper hand; to outnum

prevent.e: From Middle English preventen (“anticipate”), from Latin praeventus, perfect passive participle of praeveniō (“to anticipate”), from prae (“before”) + veniō (“to come”).
prevent.g: To stop (an outcome); to keep from (doing something).

previous.g: Prior; occurring before something else, either in time or order.

prey.e: From Middle English preye, prei, preyȝe, borrowed from Anglo-Norman and Old French preie, one of the variants of proie, from Latin praeda.
prey.g: That which is or may be seized by animals to be devoured.

prey.e: From Middle English praien, prayen, preyen, partly from the noun and partly from Old French praer, preer, earlier preder, from Late Latin praedō, collateral form of Latin praedor, from praeda (“plunder, booty, loot”) + -ō (verbal suffix).

price.e: From Middle English price (“price, prize, value, excellence”), borrowed from Old French pris, preis, from Latin pretium (“worth, price, money spent, wages, reward”); compare praise, precious, appraise, appreciate, depreciate, etc.
price.g: The cost required to gain possession of something.

prick.e: From Middle English prik, prikke, from Old English prica, pricu (“a sharp point, minute mark, spot, dot, small portion, prick”), from Proto-West Germanic *prikō, *priku, from Proto-Germanic *prikô, *prikō (“a prick, point”), of uncertain origin, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *breyǵ- (“to scrape, scratch, rub, prickle, chap”).
prick.g: A small hole or perforation, caused by piercing.

prick.e: From Middle English prikken, from Old English prician, priccan (“to prick”), from Proto-Germanic *prikōną, *prikjaną (“to pierce, prick”), of uncertain origin; perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *breyǵ- (“to scrape, scratch, rub, prickle, chap”).

pride.e: From Middle English pryde, pride, from Old English prȳde, prȳte (“pride”) (compare Old Norse prýði (“bravery, pomp”)), derivative of Old English prūd (“proud”). The verb derives from the noun, at least since the 12th century.
pride.g: The quality or state of being proud.

pride.e: From Middle English pryde, from Middle Low German lampride, from Medieval Latin lampreda.
pride.g: The small European lamprey species Petromyzon branchialis.

priest.e: From Middle English prest, preest, from Old English prēost (“priest”), from Late Latin presbyter, from Ancient Greek πρεσβύτερος (presbúteros), from πρέσβυς (présbus, “elder, older”). Reinforced in Middle English by Old French prestre, also from Latin presbyter. The Tyndale Bible uses native English elder instead.
priest.g: A religious clergyman (clergywoman, clergyperson) who is trained to perform services or sacrifices at a church or temple.

priesthood.e: From Middle English presthed, presthede, presthod, presthode, from Old English prēosthād (“priesthood”), equivalent to priest + -hood.
priesthood.g: The role or office of a priest.

priestly.e: From Middle English prestly; equivalent to priest + -ly.

prime.e: From Middle English prime, from Old French prime and its etymon, Latin prīmus (“first”), from earlier prīsmos < *prīsemos < Proto-Italic *priisemos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“beyond, before”). The noun sense "apostrophe-like symbol" originates from the fact that the symbol ′ was originally a superscript Roman numeral one.
prime.g: First in importance, degree, or rank.
An intermediate sprint within a race, usually offering a prize and/or points.

prince.e: From Middle English prince, from Anglo-Norman prince, from Latin prī̆nceps (“first, foremost (person)”), from prīmus (“first”) + capiō (“seize, take”).
prince.g: A (male) ruler, a sovereign; a king, monarch.

princess.e: From Middle English princesse, a borrowing from Anglo-Norman princesse, Old French princesse. By surface analysis, prince + -ess.
princess.g: A female member of a royal family other than a queen, especially a daughter or granddaughter of a monarch.

principal.e: From Middle English principal, from Old French principal, from Latin prīncipālis.
principal.g: Primary; most important; first level in importance.

principality.e: From Middle English principalte, principalite, from Anglo-Norman principalté, Middle French principalté, from Late Latin prīncipālitās, from Latin prīncipālis (“principal”) + -tās. Equivalent to principal + -ity.
principality.g: A region or sovereign nation headed by a prince or princess.

principle.e: From Middle English principle, from Old French principe, from Latin prīncipium (“beginning, foundation”), from prīnceps (“first”). By surface analysis, prīmus (“first”) + -ceps (“catcher”); the former ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- (“before”); see also prince.
principle.g: A fundamental assumption, fundamental law or guiding belief.

print.e: From Middle English *printen, prenten, preenten, an apheretic form of emprinten, enprinten (“to impress; imprint”) (see imprint).
print.g: Of, relating to, or writing for printed publications.

prior.e: The adverb and noun are derived from the adjective.
prior.g: Coming before in order or time; earlier, former, previous.

prior.e: From Middle English priour, prior (“head or deputy head of a monastery or other religious house; predecessor; superior”), from Old English prior, from Anglo-Norman priour, prior, priur, and Old French prior, priur (modern French prieur), and directly from their etymon Latin prior (“ancestor.
prior.g: A high-ranking member of a religious house or religious order.

prise.e: From the Middle English noun prise (“taking of something”), from Old French prise (“seizure; taking; capture”), past participle of prendre (“to take”).
prise.g: To force (open) with a lever; to pry.

prison.e: From Middle English prisoun, prison, from Old English prisūn, a borrowing from Old French prison, from Latin prehensiōnem, accusative singular of prehensiō, from the verb prehendō.
prison.g: A place or institution where people are held against their will, in the US especially for long-term confinement, as of those convicted of se

prisoner.e: From Middle English prisoner, from Old French prisonier (compare Medieval Latin prisōnārius), equivalent to prison + -er.
prisoner.g: A person incarcerated in a prison, while on trial or serving a sentence.

private.e: From Middle English privat(e) (“individual, exclusive, private”), from Latin prīvātus (“bereaved, deprived, set apart from, release”), perfect passive participle of prīvō (“to bereave, deprive, release”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more), from prīvus (“private, one's own, proper”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *per.
private.g: Belonging or pertaining to an individual person, group of people, or entity that is not the state.

privilege.e: From Middle English privilege, from Anglo-Norman privilege and Old French privilege, from Latin prīvilēgium (“ordinance or law against or in favor of an individual”), from prīvus (“private”) + lēx, lēg- (“law”).
privilege.g: An exemption from certain laws granted by the Pope.

privily.e: From Middle English prively; equivalent to privy + -ly.
privily.g: Secretly, in secret; in a private manner; privately.

privy.e: From Middle English pryvy, prive, from Old French privé (“private”), from Latin prīvātus (“deprived”), perfect passive participle of prīvō (“to bereave, deprive; to free, release”).
privy.g: Private, exclusive; not public; one's own.

prize.e: From Middle English prise, from Old French prise (“a taking, capture, a seizure, a thing seized, a prize, booty, also hold, purchase”), past participle of prendre (“to take, to capture”), from Latin prēndere (“to take, seize”); see prehend.
prize.g: That which is taken from another; something captured; a thing seized by force, stratagem, or superior power.

prize.e: From Middle English prysen, borrowed from Old French preisier (“to set a price or value on, esteem, value”), from pris (“price”), from Latin pretium (“price, value”), whence price; see also praise, a doublet.
prize.g: To consider highly valuable; to esteem.

probe.e: For verb: borrowed from Latin probare (“to test, examine, prove”), from probus (“good”). For noun: borrowed from Late Latin proba (“a proof”), from probare (“to test, examine, prove”);.
probe.g: Any of various medical instruments used to explore wounds, organs, etc.

problem.e: From Middle English probleme, from Middle French probleme, from Latin problēma, from Ancient Greek πρόβλημα (próblēma, “anything thrown forward, hindrance, obstacle, anything projecting, a headland, promontory”), from προβάλλω (probállō, “to throw or lay something in front of someone, to put forward”).
problem.g: A difficulty that has to be resolved or dealt with.

procedure.e: From French procédure, from Old French, from Latin procedere (“to go forward, proceed”); see proceed.
procedure.g: A particular method for performing a task.

proceed.e: From Middle English proceden, from Old French proceder, from Latin prōcēdō (“to go forth, go forward, advance”), from prō (“forth”) + cēdō (“to go”); see cede.
proceed.g: To move, pass, or go forward or onward; to advance; to carry on.

proceeding.g: The act of one who proceeds, or who prosecutes a design or transaction.

process.e: From Middle English proces, from Old French procés (“journey”), from Latin prōcessus (“course, progression”), nominalization of prōcēdō (“proceed, advance”).
process.g: A series of events leading to a result or product.
To walk in a procession, especially in a liturgical context.

procession.e: From Middle English processioun, borrowed from Old French pourciession, from Latin prōcessiō (“a marching forward, an advance, in Late Latin a religious procession”), from prōcēdere, past participle prōcessus (“to move forward, advance, proceed”); see proceed.
procession.g: The act of progressing or proceeding.

proclaim.e: From Middle English proclamen, proclaime, from Old French proclamer, from Latin prōclāmō, prōclāmāre, from prō- (“forth”) + clāmō (“to shout, cry out”). Spelling altered by influence of claim, from the same Latin source (clāmō).

proclamation.e: From Middle English proclamacion, from Anglo-Norman and Old French proclamacion, from Late Latin proclāmātiō, from the verb Latin prōclāmō.
proclamation.g: A statement which is proclaimed; a formal public announcement.

proconsul.g: A magistrate who served as a consul and then as the governor of a province.

procure.e: From Middle English procuren, from Old French procurer, from Late Latin prōcūrāre (“to manage, administer”), from prō (“on behalf of”) + cūrō (“to care for”).

produce.e: From Middle English produce, from Latin prōdūcō (“to lead forth”), from prō- (“forth, forward”) + dūcō (“to lead, bring”).
produce.g: To bring forth, to yield, make, manufacture, or otherwise generate.

product.e: From Middle English product, from Latin prōductus, perfect participle of prōdūcō, first attested in English in the mathematics sense.
product.g: Anything that is produced; a result.

profane.e: From Middle English prophane, from Middle French profane, prophaine, prophane and its etymon Classical Latin profānus (“not religious, unclean”) (also Late Latin prophānus), from pro- (“instead of”) + fānum (“temple”).
profane.g: Unclean; ritually impure; unholy, desecrating a holy place or thing.

profane.e: From Middle English prophanen, from Middle French profaner, prophaner and its etymon Classical Latin profānō (also Late Latin prophāno), from profānus + -ō (suffix forming verbs).
profane.g: To violate (something sacred); to treat with abuse, irreverence, obloquy, or contempt; to desecrate

profaned.e: From the past and past participle of the verb profane.
profaned.g: Treated with irreverence or without due respect.

profess.e: From Old French professer, and its source, the participle stem of Latin profitērī, from pro- + fatērī (“to confess, acknowledge”).
profess.g: To administer the vows of a religious order to (someone); to admit to a religious order.

profession.e: From Middle English professioun, from Anglo-Norman professioun, Old French profession (“declaration of faith, religious vows, occupation”), from Latin professiō (“avowal, public declaration”), from the participle stem of profitērī (“to profess”). By surface analysis, profess + -ion.

profit.e: From Middle English profit, from Old French profit (Modern French profit), from Latin prōfectus (“advance, progress, growth, increase, profit”), from proficiō (“to go forward, advance, make progress, be profitable or useful”).
profit.g: Total income or cash flow minus expenditures. The money or other benefit a non-governmental organization or individual receives in exchange

profitable.e: From Old French profitable, equivalent to profit + -able.

profound.e: From Middle English profound, profounde, from Anglo-Norman profound, from Old French profont, profonde, from Latin profundus (“deep, profound”), from prō + fundus (“bottom; foundation”).
profound.g: Descending far below the surface; opening or reaching to great depth; deep.

profound.e: From Middle English profounden, from Middle French profonder (from profond) and Medieval Latin profundāre (from profundus).
profound.g: To cause to sink deeply; to cause to dive or penetrate far down.

progenitor.e: From Middle English progenitour, from Anglo-Norman progenitour, Middle French progeniteur (Modern French progéniteur), and their etymon Latin prōgenitor, from prōgenitus, perfect participle of prōgignere (“to beget”), itself from prō- (“forth”) + gignere (“to beget”). By surface analysis, pro- (“prior, fore-”) + genitor.
progenitor.g: A forefather, any of a person's direct ancestors.

progress.e: From Middle English progresse, from Old French progres (“a going forward”), from Latin prōgressus (“an advance”), from the participle stem of prōgredī (“to go forward, advance, develop”), from pro- (“forth, before”) + gradi (“to walk, go”).
progress.g: Movement or advancement through a series of events, or points in time; development through time.

progress.e: From the noun. Lapsed into disuse in the 17th century, except in the US. Considered an Americanism on reintroduction to use in the UK.
progress.g: To move, go, or proceed forward; to advance.

prohibit.e: From Middle English prohibiten, from Latin prohibeō (“to fend off, prevent, prohibit”) (through past participle prohibitus).
prohibit.g: To forbid, disallow, or proscribe officially; to make illegal or illicit.

project.e: From Latin prōiectus, perfect passive participle of prōiciō (“throw forth, extend; expel”).
project.g: A planned endeavor, usually with a specific goal and accomplished in several steps or stages.

projection.e: From either the Middle French projection or its etymon, the Classical Latin prōiectiō (stem: prōiectiōn-), from prōiciō, equivalent to project + -ion.
projection.g: Something which projects, protrudes, juts out, sticks out, or stands out.

prolong.e: Either a back-formation from prolongation, or from Old French prolonguer or porloignier, from Latin prōlongō, from prō + longō.
prolong.g: To extend in space or length.

prominence.e: From obsolete French prominence (compare proéminence), from Latin prominentia.
prominence.g: The state of being prominent: widely known or eminent.

prominent.e: From obsolete French prominent (compare proéminent), from Latin prōminēns, present active participle of prōmineō (“jut out, to project”), from prō (“before, forward”) + mineō (in compounds, “jut, project”).
prominent.g: Standing out, or projecting; jutting; protuberant.

promiscuity.g: The state or quality of being promiscuous.

promiscuous.e: From Latin prōmiscuus (“mixed, not separated”), from prō (“forth”) + misceō (“mix”).
promiscuous.g: Made up of various disparate elements mixed together; of disorderly composition.

promise.e: From Middle English promis, promisse, borrowed from Old French promesse, from Medieval Latin prōmissa, Latin prōmissum (“a promise”), feminine and neuter past participles of prōmittō (“to send forth, to say beforehand, to promise”), from pro (“forth”) + mittere (“to send”); see mission.
promise.g: An oath or affirmation; a vow.

promote.e: From Latin prōmōtus, perfect passive participle of prōmoveō (“move forward, advance”).
promote.g: To raise (someone) to a more important, responsible, or remunerative job or rank.

promotion.e: Late Middle English, from Old French promocion, from Late Latin prōmotiō, from Latin prōmoveō (“to move forward”). Equivalent to promote + -ion.
promotion.g: An advancement in rank or position.

pronounce.e: Recorded since c.1330 as Middle English pronouncen (“to utter, declare officially”), from Old French prononcier, from Latin prōnūntiō, itself from prō- (“forth, out, in public”) + nūntiō (“to announce”) from nūntius (“messenger”).
pronounce.g: To declare formally, officially or ceremoniously.

pronouncement.e: From Anglo-Norman and Old French prononcement. By surface analysis, pronounce + -ment.

proof.e: From Middle English proof, from Old French prove, from Late Latin proba (“a proof”), from Latin probō (“to prove”); see prove; compare also the doublet probe.
proof.g: An effort, process, or operation designed to establish or discover a fact or truth; an act of testing; a test; a trial.

prop.e: From Middle English proppe (“a prop, support, support for a vine or plant”), from Middle Dutch proppe (“support, support for a vine, stopper for a bottle”).
prop.g: An object placed against or under another, to support it; anything that supports.
An item placed on a stage or set to create a scene or scenario in which actors perform.

proper.e: From Middle English propre, from Anglo-Norman proper, propre, Old French propre (French: propre), from Latin proprius.

property.e: From Middle English propertee, properte, propirte, proprete, borrowed from Anglo-Norman and Old French propreté, proprieté (“propriety, fitness, property”), from Latin proprietās (“a peculiarity, one's peculiar nature or quality, right or fact of possession, property”), from proprius (“special, particular, one's own”). Equivalent to proper + -ty.

prophecy.e: From Middle English prophecie, from Old French prophetie, from Latin prophētīa, from Ancient Greek προφητεία (prophēteía, “prophecy”), from προφήτης (prophḗtēs, “speaker of a god”), from πρό (pró, “before”) + φημί (phēmí, “to tell”).
prophecy.g: A prediction, especially one made by a prophet or under divine inspiration.

prophesied.g: Foretold or spoken of in advance.

prophesy.e: From Middle English prophecien; partly from prophecie, and partly from Middle French prophecier, prophesier, from prophecie (“prophecy”).
prophesy.g: To speak or write with divine inspiration; to act as prophet.
Obsolete spelling of prophecy; now a misspelling.

prophet.e: From Middle English prophete, from Anglo-Norman prophete, from Latin prophēta, from Ancient Greek προφήτης (prophḗtēs, “one who speaks for a god”), from πρό (pró, “before”) + φημί (phēmí, “to tell”).
prophet.g: Someone who speaks by divine inspiration.

prophetess.e: From Middle English prophetesse, from Old French prophetesse, from Late Latin prophetissa. By surface analysis, prophet + -ess.

propitiation.e: From Middle English propiciacion, propiciacioun, from Anglo-Norman propiciatiun, Middle French propiciation, propitiation, and their etymon Latin propitiātiō (stem propitiātiōn-). By surface analysis, propitiate + -ion.
propitiation.g: The act of propitiating; placation, atonement, similar to expiation but also involving the appeasement of anger.

proportion.e: From Middle English proporcion, from Old French proportion, from Latin prōportiō (“comparative relation, proportion, symmetry, analogy”), from pro (“for, before”) + portio (“share, part”); see portion. By surface analysis, pro- + portion.
proportion.g: A quantity of something that is part of the whole amount or number.

propose.e: From Middle English proposen, from Anglo-Norman proposer (verb), propos (noun), Middle French proposer (verb), propos (noun), from Latin prōpōnō, prōpōnere, with conjugation altered based on poser.
propose.g: To suggest a plan, course of action, etc.

prosecute.e: Borrowed from Latin prōsecūtus, perfect participle of prōsequor.

prosecution.e: From Middle French prosecution and its etymon Late Latin prōsecutio, from Latin prōsequor (“follow, pursue”), from pro- (“onward”) + sequor (“follow”, whence English sequel). By surface analysis, prosecute + -ion.
prosecution.g: The act of prosecuting a scheme or endeavor.

proselyte.e: From Old French proselite, from Late Latin proselytus (“proselyte, alien resident”), from Ancient Greek προσήλυτος (prosḗlutos, “newcomer, convert”) (from πρός (prós, “to, towards”) and the stem -ηλυ- of ἐλήλυθα (elḗlutha), perfect of ἔρχομαι (érkhomai, “come”)), translation of Hebrew גר (ger) in the Septuagint translation of the Torah (e.g., Exodus 12:49).
proselyte.g: One who has converted to a religion or doctrine, especially a gentile converted to Judaism.

prospect.e: From Middle English prospecte, from Latin prōspectus (“view, sight, prospect; panorama”), from prōspiciō (“to look forward”) + -tus (suffix forming action nouns), from pro (“before, forward”) + speciō, spiciō (“to look, to see”). By surface analysis, pro- + -spect. Etymology 1, noun sense 11 is a semantic loan from Russian проспе́кт (prospékt).
prospect.g: The region which the eye overlooks at one time; a view; a scene; an outlook.
To have or afford a view; to face or look out.

prosper.e: From Old French prosperer, from Latin prosperō (“to render happy”), from prosperus (“prosperous”), from Proto-Italic *prosparos, from Proto-Indo-European *speh₁- (“to succeed”), whence also Latin spēs (“hope, expectation”).
prosper.g: To be successful; to succeed; to be fortunate or prosperous; to thrive; to make gain.

prosperity.e: From Middle English prosperite, from Old French prosperitet, from Latin prosperitās, equivalent to prosper + -ity.
prosperity.g: The condition of being prosperous: having good fortune and a fortune.

prosperous.e: From Middle French prospereus, from Old French prosperer, from Latin prosperō (“to cause to succeed”), from Old Latin pro spere (“according to expectation”), from pro (“for”) + spes (“hope”).

prostitute.e: From Latin prōstitūtus, past participle of prōstituō, from prō̆ (“for, before”) + statuō (“to set up, to erect”).
prostitute.g: Debased, corrupt; seeking personal gain by dishonourable means.

prostitution.e: From Late Latin prostitutio. Equivalent to prostitute + -ion.
prostitution.g: Engaging in sexual activity with another person for pay.

protect.e: Largely displaced native Middle English shelden, from Old English sċildan (“to protect,” literally “to shield”).
protect.g: To keep safe; to defend; to guard; to prevent harm coming to.

protection.e: From Middle English, from Old French, from stem of Late Latin prōtectiō (“a covering over”), from Latin prōtēctus, perfect passive participle of prōtegere (“to protect, cover in front”). Equivalent to protect + -ion.
protection.g: The process of keeping (something or someone) safe.

protective.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin prōtēctīvus. By surface analysis, protect + -ive.

protest.e: From the Middle English verb protesten, from Old French protester, from Latin prōtestārī, from prō + testor, from testis (“witness”).

protract.e: From the past participle stem of Latin prōtrahō. By surface analysis, pro- + tract.
protract.g: To draw out; to extend, especially in duration.

protrude.e: Borrowed from Latin prōtrūdere, the present active infinitive of prōtrūdō (“to push or thrust forwards; to protrude”), from prō- (“prefix denoting a forward direction or movement”) (from Proto-Indo-European *pro- (“forward; toward”)) + trūdō (“to push, shove, thrust”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *trewd- (“to push, thrust”)).
protrude.g: To cause (something) to extend above, beyond, or from a boundary or surface; to cause (something) to project or stick out.

proud.e: From Middle English proud, prout, prut, from Old English prūd, prūt (“proud, arrogant, haughty”) (compare Old English prȳtung (“pride”); prȳde, prȳte (“pride”), see also Old English deal), probably from Old French prod, prut (“brave, gallant”) (modern French preux), from Late Latin prōde (“useful”), derived from Latin prōdesse (“to be of value”).
proud.g: Feeling honoured (by something); feeling happy or satisfied about an event or fact; gratified.

proudly.e: From Middle English proutly, proudliche, prudeliche, prudliche, prouteliche, from Old English prūtlīċe, equivalent to proud + -ly.

prove.e: Simple past form of proove, conjugated as a Germanic strong verb, on the pattern of choose → chose.

proven.e: From Scottish English, as past participle of preve, a Middle English variant of prove – compare woven (from weave) and cloven (from cleave), both of which feature -eve → -oven.
proven.g: Having been proved; having proved its value or truth.

provender.e: From Middle English provendre, from Old French provendre, variant of provende (“allowance, provision”), from Late Latin praebenda (“a payment, in Medieval Latin also an allowance of food and drink, pittance, also a prebend”).

proverb.e: From Old French proverbe, from Latin proverbium.
proverb.g: A commonly used sentence expressing popular wisdom.

provide.e: From Middle English providen, from Latin prōvidēre (“to foresee, act with foresight”).
provide.g: To make a living; earn money for necessities.

providence.e: From Middle English providence, from Anglo-Norman providence, Middle French providence, and their source, Latin prōvidentia (“providence, foresight”), from the present participle of prōvidēre (“to provide”). By surface analysis, provide + -ence.
providence.g: Preparation for the future; good governance; foresight.

province.e: From Middle English provynce, from Anglo-Norman province, Old French province, from Latin prōvincia, seemingly corresponding to prō- (“forward”) + vinciō (“to bind, bind about, fetter, tie, fasten, surround, encircle”).
province.g: A region of the earth or of a continent; a district or country.

proving.e: From Middle English provyng, pryvynge, equivalent to prove + -ing.

provision.e: From Middle English provisioun, from Old French provisïon, from Latin prōvīsiō (“preparation, foresight”), from prōvidēre (“provide”).
provision.g: An item of goods or supplies, especially food, obtained for future use.

provocation.e: From Middle English provocacioun, from Old French provocacion, from Late Latin prōvocātiō, prōvocātiōnem, from Latin prōvocō. By surface analysis, provoke + -ation.
provocation.g: The act of provoking, inciting or annoying someone into doing something.

provoke.e: Borrowed from Middle French provoquer, from Old French, from Latin prōvocāre.
provoke.g: To cause someone to become annoyed or angry.

prowl.e: From Middle English prollen, of unknown origin.
prowl.g: To rove over, through, or about in a stealthy manner; especially, to search in, as for prey or booty.

prudence.e: From Middle English prudence (“discretion; foresight; knowledge; intelligence, wisdom; act of good judgment; wisdom to see what is virtuous”), from Anglo-Norman prudence, Middle French prudence, and Old French prudence (“common sense; wisdom”) (modern French prudence), and from their etymon Latin prūdentia (“common sense; discretion, prudence; foresight.
prudence.g: The quality or state of being prudent: circumspection and good judgment in knowing how best to act; (countable, archaic) an instance of this

prudent.e: From Middle English prudent, from Old French prudent, from Latin prūdēns, contracted from prōvidēns (“foresight”) (English providence), the present participle of prōvideō (“to forsee; to provide for”). Unrelated to prude.
prudent.g: Sagacious in adapting means to ends; circumspect in action, or in determining any line of conduct.

prune.e: From Middle English prune, from Old French prune, from Vulgar Latin *prūna, feminine singular formed from the neutral plural of Latin prūnum, from Ancient Greek προῦνον (proûnon), variant of προῦμνον (proûmnon, “plum”), a loanword from a language of Asia Minor.

From Middle English prunen, prounen, proinen, from Old French proignier (“to trim the feathers with the beak”), earlier prooignier. Likely influenced by Middle French rogner, Old French rooignier (“cut, trim”) (from Latin rotundo?), and possibly by Old French provainier (“provine”) (Latin propaginem? whence French provigner).
prune.g: To remove excess material from a tree or shrub; to trim, especially to make more healthy or productive.
